title: The Navy Made Him Serve Meals. At Pearl Harbor, He Manned a Machine Gun.

beats.text: On the morning of December 7, 1941, a young sailor was collecting laundry on a battleship at Pearl Harbor.

overlays.hook: He was collecting laundry. *Then Pearl Harbor.*

beats.text: The Navy had given him one kind of job. Feed the officers. Serve their meals. It was the only branch open to a Black recruit.
Before that morning was over, he was behind a machine gun, firing at Japanese planes. He had never been trained to use it.
The Navy praised his courage, but it did not give his name. A Black newspaper had to find it.
He became the first Black sailor to receive the Navy Cross. And he still went back to work as a mess attendant.

visual.caption: Admiral Nimitz pins the Navy Cross on Doris Miller, 27 May 1942

beats.text: His name was Doris Miller. History knows him as Dorie. This is the story of the sailor the Navy was not ready for.
Doris Miller was born on October 12, 1919, in Waco, Texas.
His parents were farmers, and he was one of four sons. He worked the land with his family.
He grew up big and strong, and he played fullback on his high school football team.
But he left school without graduating. His family needed the money, and there were few good jobs around Waco for a young Black man.
So he looked to the Navy, for steady pay and a way out of Waco.

visual.title: The U.S. Navy
visual.sub: steady pay, and a way out

beats.text: On September 16, 1939, two weeks after war broke out in Europe, he walked into a recruiting station in Dallas and signed up for six years.
He was nineteen years old.
But the Navy had a separate place for men like him.
At that time, a Black recruit had almost no choice. He went into the messman branch.
Messmen fed and served the white officers. They looked after their meals and their laundry. It was a segregated branch, made up mostly of Black and Filipino sailors.
White sailors were not allowed to serve in it. And for Black sailors, there was almost no way out of it.
Miller enlisted as a mess attendant, third class. He trained at Norfolk, Virginia, and was sent to the ammunition ship Pyro.
Then, on January 2, 1940, he joined the crew of the battleship USS West Virginia.
On a ship full of men, he made his name another way. He became the heavyweight boxing champion of the West Virginia.
His battle station, if the alarm ever rang, was below decks, at an ammunition magazine serving the anti-aircraft guns.

visual.caption: USS West Virginia, inboard and outboard profiles, 1930s

beats.text: He would pass the ammunition. Other men would do the fighting.
Sunday, December 7, 1941. Pearl Harbor, Hawaii.
West Virginia was moored along Battleship Row, with the rest of the Pacific Fleet around her.
Just before eight in the morning, Dorie Miller was below decks, collecting laundry.
Then Japanese planes came in over the harbor.
The first torpedo hit West Virginia. Then more. Water poured into the ship.
Miller ran for his battle station. He found it destroyed.
There was no ammunition to pass. So he started helping the injured men he could reach.
An officer sent him up to the bridge. The captain of the West Virginia, Mervyn Bennion, had been badly wounded.
Miller was the ship's boxing champion. He and others carried the captain to a safer spot behind the conning tower.
Captain Bennion did not survive the attack.
Then came the moment people still remember.
Near the conning tower stood fifty-caliber anti-aircraft machine guns. Miller was told to help feed them ammunition.
Then he took one of the guns himself.

visual.caption: "Above and Beyond the Call of Duty", U.S. Navy poster, 1943

beats.text: He had never been trained on it. A mess attendant was not supposed to be there.
He aimed at the planes and fired, and he kept firing until the ammunition ran out.
Afterward, he made it sound simple. It was not hard, he said. I just pulled the trigger, and she worked fine.

visual.quote: I just pulled the trigger, and she worked fine.

beats.text: How many planes he hit is still argued over. He believed he hit one. The Navy never settled it.
And it almost does not matter. A man the Navy had trained to serve meals was shooting back.
West Virginia could not be saved. She settled onto the bottom of the harbor, on fire.
Miller helped pull sailors out of the water.
More than a hundred men of the West Virginia were lost that morning.

visual.sub: men of the West Virginia lost

beats.text: Across Pearl Harbor, more than two thousand Americans died. The next day, the United States went to war.
A few days later, Miller was transferred to the cruiser USS Indianapolis. He was back at work as a mess attendant.

visual.title: USS Indianapolis
visual.sub: back at work as a mess attendant

beats.text: Meanwhile, a story began to spread about a Black sailor at Pearl Harbor who had manned a machine gun.
Newspapers carried it before the month was out. There was no name.
On January 1, 1942, the Navy issued a commendation for the sailor. It still did not name him.
Black Americans wanted to know who he was. And they wanted to know why the Navy would not say.
The Pittsburgh Courier, one of the leading Black newspapers in the country, went looking for him.
In March 1942, it printed his name. It called him Dorie Miller. And that is the name that stuck.
Now the pressure grew. Bills went to Congress calling for the Medal of Honor, the highest award there is.
Navy Secretary Frank Knox recommended against it.
On May 11, 1942, President Roosevelt approved a different award: the Navy Cross.
On May 27, 1942, sailors stood in lines on the flight deck of the carrier USS Enterprise, at Pearl Harbor.
Admiral Chester Nimitz, commander of the Pacific Fleet, stepped up to Dorie Miller and pinned the medal on his chest.

visual.caption: Nimitz and Miller on the USS Enterprise

beats.text: The citation praised his distinguished devotion to duty, extraordinary courage, and disregard for his own personal safety.

visual.quote: Distinguished devotion to duty, extraordinary courage and disregard for his own personal safety.

beats.text: He was the first Black sailor ever to receive it.

visual.caption: Doris Miller receives the Navy Cross

beats.text: The Navy was starting to change, slowly. That April, it had said Black recruits could train for general service, at a new camp named for Robert Smalls, the man who sailed a Confederate ship to freedom.
But Dorie Miller, now a national hero, was still a mess attendant.
Late in 1942, after nearly a year at sea, he was brought back, and the Navy sent him on a tour.
For more than two months, he spoke to crowds and to sailors, and helped sell war bonds.
In January 1943, he stood at Great Lakes, Illinois, in front of the first class of Black recruits to graduate from Camp Robert Smalls.

visual.caption: Doris Miller at Naval Station Great Lakes, January 1943

beats.text: They were training for jobs he had never been offered.
That year, the Navy put his face on a recruiting poster. Above and beyond the call of duty, it said.

visual.caption: "Above and Beyond the Call of Duty", 1943

beats.text: Then it sent him back to sea.
In the spring of 1943, Miller joined a new escort carrier, the USS Liscome Bay.
He was promoted to cook, third class. It was a higher rank, in the same kitchen.
In November, Liscome Bay sailed for the Gilbert Islands in the Pacific, for the invasion of Makin.
On November 24, 1943, a Japanese submarine fired a torpedo into her side.
The blast set off the bombs stored aboard. The ship went down in about twenty-three minutes.
More than six hundred men were lost. Dorie Miller was one of them.
He was twenty-four years old. His body was never recovered.
Four months after he died, in March 1944, the Navy commissioned its first thirteen Black officers.
It came too late for the man who had helped force the question.
In 1973, the Navy commissioned a ship in his name, the USS Miller.
She sailed for eighteen years.
In 2010, he appeared on a United States postage stamp, among the distinguished sailors of the Navy.
And on January 20, 2020, Martin Luther King Day, the Navy announced that a future aircraft carrier would be named USS Doris Miller.

visual.caption: The USS Doris Miller announcement, 20 January 2020

beats.text: It would be the first aircraft carrier named for a Black American, and the first named for an enlisted sailor.
In 2026, reports said the Navy was weighing a new name for that ship, and that the Medal of Honor was under consideration. So far, nothing has been announced.
The first bills for his Medal of Honor went to Congress in 1942. People are still asking.
A farm boy from Waco, who wanted a way out.
A sailor the Navy would let serve meals, but not much more.
A hero it praised before it would name him, and sent back to the kitchen after it did.
Nobody had trained him for that gun. He fired back anyway.
That was Dorie Miller. Subscribe for more.

notUsed: Number of planes hit: claims range from one to six; the script says it is argued over.
Crew lost on West Virginia: 130 (HistoryNet) vs 106 (Mental Floss): script says more than a hundred.
Liscome Bay dead: 644 (HistoryNet) vs 702 (Wikipedia): script says more than six hundred.

Gun training: he attended a secondary-battery gunnery school on USS Nevada (HistoryNet, NHHC), which was not the .50-caliber gun; several sources say no training on that weapon, and Wikipedia also says officers instructed him during the attack.
The "Dorie" typo story: the origin is uncertain. The script only says the Courier used the name and it stuck.
His mother recognising the story; the "busboy" quote; Delano and Johnson by name: single source.
Who else may be named for CVN-81 in the reports: left out on purpose. Re-check for any Navy announcement before publishing.
